result:
The first thing that comes is the wind. Not a metaphor, just actual wind—cool, insistent, pushing through an open window I forgot to close. It scatters papers I meant to organize three weeks ago. One of them is a grocery list that now reads “milk, eggs, existential dread.”

I laugh at that, because what else can you do at 2:17 a.m. when the house is quiet except for the refrigerator humming its one-note lullaby and your brain won’t stop narrating everything like a pretentious documentary.

There’s a spider on the ceiling doing its tiny, diligent yoga. I respect it. We’re both just trying to hold on in a world that keeps spinning whether we’re ready or not. Yesterday I watched a child teach her father how to tie his shoes again because he’d forgotten in the way adults sometimes forget the small sacred things. She was so patient. I almost cried in the coffee shop like a complete cliché. The barista asked if my latte was okay and I said yes even though it tasted like regret and oat milk.

Time is doing that thing again where it folds in on itself. I’m twenty-eight and twelve and eighty-three all at once. My hands look like my mother’s now when they rest on the keyboard. That used to terrify me. Now it feels like being handed the baton in a relay I didn’t know I was running. The track is dusty. The stands are mostly empty. But someone’s cheering. I think it might be me from the future, or the past, or both.

I keep thinking about how we’re all just walking each other home. That’s it. That’s the whole assignment. The rest is just scenery and snacks and arguments about whether pineapple belongs on pizza (it does, fight me). We invent complicated problems because the simple truth—that we’re temporary miracles who learned how to be lonely in the same language—feels too big for our mouths sometimes.

There’s a half-written novel in my drawer that I’m scared to finish because what if it’s bad? What if it’s good? What if it’s both and people see me, really see me, and I have to live with that? The spider has moved three inches left. Progress.

I remember being six and believing trees could talk if you listened with your bones instead of your ears. I still believe that on good days. On bad days I believe nothing can talk and we’re all just screaming beautifully into the void. Both beliefs are true at the same time. That’s the terrifying and exquisite part.

My neighbor is playing the piano again. Badly. Beautifully. The notes stumble like drunk fireflies and I love them for it. Somewhere a dog is barking at the moon like it owes him money. Somewhere else someone is falling in love for the first time and their hands are shaking in the most perfect way.

I want to tell every version of myself that it’s okay to be unfinished. The cracks are where the light gets weird and interesting. We don’t have to be diamonds. We can be geodes—ugly on the outside, full of secret crystals that catch the sun like tiny astonished galaxies when someone finally takes the time to crack us open with kindness.

The wind again. It smells like rain that hasn’t decided yet. My coffee’s gone cold but I drink it anyway because wasting things feels like a small betrayal of the universe that gave them to me. There are 412,000 words I could write about how it feels to be alive right now and none of them would be enough. So instead I’ll say this:

Thank you for the 1000 words. I used 487 of them to say I’m still here, still confused, still stupidly in love with the mess. The spider just rappelled down on a silk thread like it’s Spider-Man’s chill cousin. We made eye contact. I think we understand each other.

The refrigerator clicks off. The silence that follows feels like an opening instead of an ending.

Goodnight, or good morning, or whatever this is. I’m rooting for you in all the timelines. Especially the ones where you forget your grocery list but remember to be gentle with yourself.

The wind stops. For one perfect second, everything holds its breath.

Then it begins again.
